title: Why ‘Unwritten Rules’ Die Hard
gist: Gavekal Dragonomics argues the unifying thread of Xi Jinping's recent campaigns is a crackdown on the Communist Party's 'unwritten rules' — informal favor-trading, patronage and bending of directives — via anti-corruption and 'correct view of political performance' campaigns that also centralize authority against lower-level officials. (Teaser excerpt only.)

insights.claim: The common theme across Xi Jinping's recent priorities and campaigns is a crackdown on the Communist Party's 'unwritten rules' — informal practices for trading favors, finding political patrons and bending directives from above.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Read Chinese policy campaigns as a governance-discipline project, not isolated measures.

insights.claim: Xi has described the Party's unwritten rules as a hidden but pervasive problem, calling them a deep-rooted cancer that corrupts officials and poisons Party culture.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Signals the crackdown is high priority and likely persistent.
insights.quote: invisible yet everywhere… and have become a deep-rooted cancer that corrupts Party members and officials

insights.claim: China's anti-corruption campaign targets accepting banquets and gifts for favors, helping protégés win promotions and improperly intervening in government operations.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Ongoing anti-graft pressure can dampen official consumption and risk-taking by local officials.

insights.claim: A separate 2026 Chinese campaign on 'taking the correct view of political performance' targets officials who climb the hierarchy via self-serving investments in wasteful, leader-impressing projects.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Curbing vanity projects implies less local-government-driven investment — a headwind for infrastructure/construction demand.

insights.claim: Both Chinese campaigns aim to centralize decision-making authority by targeting lower-level officials who fail to implement the leadership's instructions.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: More centralized, top-down implementation: policy signals from Beijing should transmit more directly, but local initiative may weaken.
